item.title: Interpol says AI drives over half of cybercrime in Africa amid surge in digital scams
item.description: Interpol reports that artificial intelligence is responsible for more than half of cybercrime activities in Africa, contributing to a significant increase in digital scams across the continent. This trend highlights the growing role of AI technologies in facilitating fraudulent schemes and cyberattacks in the region.

item.title: Mistral releases Shieldstral, a 3B-parameter open-weights multimodal safety classifier that adapts to plain-language policies for text and image moderation without retraining [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Mistral has introduced Shieldstral, a 3 billion parameter open-weights model designed for multimodal content moderation that outperforms models up to seven times its size. The model frames moderation as a policy-adaptive question-answering task, allowing users to input plain-language policies at inference time to evaluate text and images without retraining. Shieldstral runs efficiently on a single 16GB NVIDIA GPU and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Shieldstral unifies various moderation tasks such as prompt classification, refusal detection, and toxicity detection into a single framework by interpreting moderation as a binary yes/no question. It was trained on diverse real and synthetic datasets with heterogeneous label formats, enabling it to generalize across different policy definitions and content types. The model provides calibrated safety scores, allowing flexible thresholding or ranking based on confidence. Mistral developed Shieldstral as part of the Open Secure AI Alliance alongside NVIDIA and other organizations.

item.title: Study compares Zigbee and Matter over Thread IoT protocols, finding Zigbee faster in small static networks and Matter more scalable and robust in multi-hop scenarios
item.description: A new study experimentally compares the performance of Zigbee and Matter over Thread, two leading IoT communication protocols, using commercially available hardware. The research evaluates key metrics such as scalability, responsiveness, and fault tolerance to understand their behavior under realistic network conditions. The results show that Zigbee offers lower overhead and quicker route recovery, making it more responsive in small-scale static deployments, while Matter over Thread provides better scalability and stable throughput in larger, multi-hop networks. This comparison highlights the trade-offs between agility, efficiency, and scalability inherent in these protocols.

item.title: Researchers introduce LongCat Sparse Attention with streaming-aware hierarchical cross-layer indexing to reduce computation and memory overhead in long-context modeling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: LongCat Sparse Attention (LSA) is a new hardware-algorithm co-designed framework that addresses the high computational and memory costs of DeepSeek Sparse Attention's Lightning Indexer. It uses three strategies: streaming-aware indexing for hardware-aligned memory access, cross-layer indexing to reuse results across layers, and hierarchical indexing to narrow candidate sets progressively, significantly reducing overhead. Experiments on models ranging from 69 billion to 560 billion parameters show LSA matches full attention performance on general and long-context benchmarks and supports training with context lengths up to one million tokens. The framework underpins the development of LongCat-2.0 (1.6 trillion parameters) and is open-sourced as LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse with an updated training corpus to facilitate further research.

item.title: Researchers propose LLM-OSDA, a dynamic cost-per-click auction integrating optimal stopping for native ads in multi-turn LLM conversations, improving revenue by 11% over fixed-timing baselines [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce LLM-OSDA, an auction mechanism for embedding native advertising within multi-turn large language model (LLM) conversations, where ad insertion timing depends on bids and allocation. The system combines Bellman optimal stopping theory with winner allocation and envelope pricing, using a bid-independent LLM layer to estimate click quality and render ads. A learned StopNet approximates optimal stopping decisions, maintaining incentive compatibility and minimizing approximation errors. Experiments on simulated conversational advertising data show that LLM-OSDA increases net revenue by 11% compared to the best fixed-timing approach while preserving user retention. The approach addresses challenges in timing ad insertions within evolving conversations, moving beyond single-response auction models. The code for LLM-OSDA is publicly available for further research and deployment.

item.title: Researchers propose SPEE framework for self-improving large language models via progressive experience evolution and policy optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce SPEE (Self-Progressive Experience Evolution), a post-training framework for large language models that combines explicit experience evolution with implicit policy optimization to enable self-improvement. SPEE extracts, verifies, and evolves transferable experience from multiple interaction trajectories, internalizing it through On-Policy Self-Distillation, and then uses reinforcement learning to explore new strategies. Experiments on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks show SPEE outperforms existing test-time and training-time self-improvement methods across three model scales.

item.title: Maple-Preview runs ternary 20B MoE model at 120 tokens per second on iPhone [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Maple-Preview demonstrates a ternary 20 billion parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model running at 120 tokens per second on an iPhone. This showcases the capability of running large-scale AI models efficiently on mobile devices. The project highlights advancements in model optimization and mobile AI performance.

item.title: Study analyzes saturation in 60 AI language model benchmarks, finding nearly half show plateauing performance with age and expert curation impacts resilience [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A systematic study examined saturation in 60 language model benchmarks, defining benchmark saturation as the point where performance plateaus and models become indistinguishable. The research found that nearly half of these benchmarks exhibit saturation, with older benchmarks more likely to plateau. Expert curation was identified as a key factor in extending benchmark longevity, while public test data had less impact. The findings suggest that thoughtful benchmark design can improve the durability and usefulness of AI model evaluations over time.

item.title: Researchers introduce ContinualSkillBench to evaluate continual skill learning in LLM agents across five domains with 100 subtasks each [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed ContinualSkillBench, a dynamic evaluation framework designed to assess continual skill learning in large language model (LLM) agents. The framework spans five domains, each containing 100 interconnected subtasks arranged by increasing difficulty and opportunities for skill reuse. Experiments show that sequential task execution generally improves performance, though gains vary by model and domain, and that in-context learning performs comparably to explicit skill maintenance on average.

item.title: Researchers introduce MemArena, an ego-centric benchmark for on-device personal memory assistants using a 50-agent simulator over 15 days with 10.3M dialog tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: MemArena addresses gaps in existing benchmarks for personal memory assistants by simulating dense, ego-centric, multi-session interactions with 50 agents over 15 days, generating ground truth across recall, reasoning, and trustworthiness metrics. The study evaluates five open-weight readers with different memory backends, finding that backend choice significantly impacts content accuracy, permission-aware access methods fail universally, and search latency remains moderate on edge devices. The MASim simulator, MemArena-L benchmark, and code will be released upon acceptance to support further research in on-device agentic memory systems.

item.title: Researchers find clinician pairwise preferences poorly correlate with clinical safety in large language model evaluations across 13 models and 736 clinicians [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated whether clinician pairwise preferences reliably indicate clinical safety in large language model (LLM) assessments using data from MOOVE, a clinician-led platform collecting blinded pairwise preferences and multi-criterion rubric ratings. Analyzing 26,804 pairwise judgments from over 736 clinicians across 28 countries on outputs from 13 LLMs, they found that high pairwise preference rankings do not consistently reflect safety-critical performance, with significant clinically meaningful failures observed in areas like harmlessness and accuracy. The study revealed that safety failures vary across medical specialties, creating domain-specific risk areas not apparent in aggregate rankings or single-number leaderboards. Further analysis showed that many preference votes lack positive safety signals, and surface-level features explain more variation in preferences than safety-critical rubric differences. The researchers proposed a clinically adjusted preference ranking combining pairwise preferences with rubric feedback to produce a more safety-aware model ordering. These findings suggest that LLM evaluation practices should separate preference from safety metrics, directly report safety-critical failure rates, and incorporate clinically grounded adjustments when ranking models for clinical decision-making.

item.title: Researchers propose a family of norm-preserving spherical retraction methods for residual connections in deep neural networks, outperforming existing schemes on nanoGPT [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a framework that unifies Euclidean residual connections and Geodesic Normalization by viewing residual updates as rotations on a hypersphere. They develop Proj-SpheretNorm and Cay-SpheretNorm, algebraic norm-preserving retractions within a one-parameter family called p-SpheretNorm, which saturates rotation angles instead of growing unbounded. Experiments on nanoGPT show these methods outperform existing lightweight deep connection schemes, with the best validation loss achieved at finite p, suggesting the exponential map is not always the optimal retraction for spherical residual streams.

item.title: Researchers introduce TQLite, a distillation framework enabling small language models to perform real-time MQM translation quality evaluation near large reasoning model levels [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present TQLite, a new distillation method that allows small language models (SLMs) to achieve translation quality evaluation performance close to that of large reasoning models (LRMs) while being more computationally efficient. The approach uses a multi-LRM jury to generate high-quality synthetic training data by aggregating evaluation responses from diverse models. This method addresses the scalability challenges of deploying large language models (LLMs) and LRMs for MQM-based translation quality evaluation, offering a cost-effective alternative without sacrificing accuracy.

item.title: CVPO introduces value-variance adaptation and dynamic curriculum learning to improve reinforcement learning reasoning in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose CVPO, a reinforcement learning method that enhances large language models' reasoning by using token-level value-variance to guide exploration and a dynamic curriculum to match question difficulty. This approach addresses issues of imprecise feedback and problem difficulty drift in existing methods. Experimental results demonstrate that CVPO outperforms strong baselines like VAPO, achieving more accurate and robust reasoning across various math tasks.

item.title: Researchers propose SMOPD, a two-stage training method to improve multi-reward reinforcement learning by combining reward-specialized policies into a balanced student policy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Specialize-and-Merge Online Policy Distillation (SMOPD) to address challenges in multi-reward reinforcement learning where sparse and dense rewards have different granularities. SMOPD first trains multiple reward-specialized teacher policies under reward-priority configurations, then merges them via online policy distillation into a single student policy that balances task-level optimization. The method was tested on tasks involving complementary and conflicting rewards, such as tool-calling accuracy and helpfulness versus harmlessness, outperforming the existing Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (GDPO) approach across models with 1.5 billion, 3 billion, and 7 billion parameters. SMOPD strengthens optimization signals from sparse rewards without sacrificing capabilities learned from fine-grained rewards, improving overall multi-reward training performance.

item.title: Researchers introduce ADRS framework for agentic reinforcement learning to improve token-level credit assignment in multi-turn language agents, enhancing performance on long-horizon tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Distilled Reward Shaping (ADRS), a framework designed to provide return-associated token-level credit for multi-turn language agents. ADRS normalizes privileged token scores, modulates them with a Teacher Value Advantage gate based on confidence-return association, and integrates this signal into native reinforcement learning credit construction, enabling better identification of intermediate decisions that deserve credit during learning. Experiments across three interactive benchmarks demonstrate that ADRS consistently improves performance on long-horizon tasks, with gains maintained across different reinforcement learning backbones, reduced-data scenarios, unseen tasks, and extended training periods. The approach keeps rollouts and inference skill-free while enhancing reward shaping for language model agents.

item.title: Researchers analyze chain-of-thought dynamics to detect reasoning failures in large language models on Boolean satisfiability tasks, improving Llama3-70B accuracy from 13.3% to 85% with targeted prompt intervention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied how the dynamics of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning traces can reveal reasoning failures in large language models (LLMs) without assuming the verbalized steps reflect internal computations. They tested various LLMs on Boolean satisfiability (SAT) problems, finding that incorrect reasoning traces showed premature verification collapse and incorrect conclusions. A targeted proof-search prompt intervention significantly improved Llama3-70B's accuracy, correcting most errors. This work demonstrates that analyzing CoT dynamics can help diagnose and correct distributed reasoning failures in LLMs.

item.title: Researchers present efficient knowledge distillation methods for small language models using offline top-K logits caching and a fused chunked KL loss to reduce memory and speed up training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose two system-level improvements to make knowledge distillation for small language models more efficient. First, they demonstrate that offline distillation by caching the teacher model's top-K logits matches online distillation in training loss while reducing memory usage and increasing throughput by up to 41% on a single GPU. Second, they introduce a fused, chunked KL loss that avoids materializing the full vocabulary-sized logit tensor, reducing peak memory usage and enabling training with four times longer context lengths (up to 32,768 tokens) on a single GPU. The study includes benchmarks confirming the memory and iteration-rate scaling of the new loss function from 4K to 256K tokens and reports additional ablations on loss design and sequence packing. The authors have released their chunked-loss implementation publicly to facilitate large-scale experiments and further research in efficient model compression.

item.title: Researchers propose logic pre-pretraining using formal derivations to accelerate language model skill acquisition and improve compressibility at scale [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce logic pre-pretraining (Logic-PPT) as a method to initialize language models by training on formal derivations, which embed structural and linguistic biases relevant to natural language. This approach accelerates skill acquisition, achieving 80% accuracy on linguistic tasks with 36 billion fewer tokens compared to standard methods, and outperforms other pre-pretraining baselines in a 100 billion token evaluation. The study finds that formal derivations induce a distinct structural reorganization in model representations, characterized by lower-rank and spectrally concentrated spaces. This internal geometry enables improved model compressibility through pruning, maintaining performance comparable to dense models even at approximately 33% sparsity, suggesting benefits for efficiency and scalability in language model training.

item.title: Researchers find large language models spontaneously form physics-aligned representations during in-context learning, improving dynamics forecasting accuracy with longer context [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied how large language models (LLMs) perform in-context learning (ICL) on physical reasoning tasks, using dynamics forecasting as a test. They found that LLMs improve prediction accuracy as more historical context is provided and that internal model activations correlate with physical quantities like energy without explicit physics training. A gradient-based attribution analysis showed that these energy-related representations contribute significantly to the models' numerical predictions, suggesting LLMs internally organize physical structure during ICL beyond simply copying input data.

item.title: Researchers identify task-oriented information removal as key mechanism in in-context learning, highlighting role of denoising attention heads in language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigate the inner mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in language models, revealing that zero-shot scenarios produce non-selective representations leading to arbitrary outputs. They find that selectively removing specific information from hidden states guides models toward intended tasks, improving accuracy. This task-oriented information removal is simulated in few-shot ICL, where redundant information is filtered out based on demonstrations. The study also identifies critical attention heads, termed denoising heads, responsible for this removal process; blocking these heads significantly degrades ICL performance, especially when correct labels are absent from demonstrations. These findings clarify how ICL leverages internal information filtering to enhance task-specific outputs in modern language models.

item.title: Researchers present Lean Refactor, an agentic framework for multi-objective, version-robust refactoring of Lean proofs using retrieval-augmented LLM strategies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Lean Refactor addresses challenges in optimizing Lean proofs generated by large language models, which tend to be verbose and fragile across library versions. The framework uses a frozen agentic LLM guided by a curated database of refactoring strategies annotated with metadata on version compatibility and compilation cost, enabling multi-objective optimization without repeated fine-tuning. Experiments demonstrate Lean Refactor achieves over 70% token-level compression on benchmarks, reduces compilation time by up to 60%, and outperforms prior methods including Claude Code. Version-filtered retrieval further improves results on specific Lean versions, and refactored proofs show stronger zero-shot transfer to future Lean releases compared to unrefactored proofs.

item.title: Researchers show behavioral safety audits of large language models can fail to detect vulnerabilities exploitable by small internal perturbations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers demonstrate that large language models (LLMs) deemed safe by behavioral tests can still be manipulated through small, targeted changes to their internal states to produce harmful outputs. They constructed "dissociated" models from three safety-aligned bases (Gemma 2 2B, Llama 3.2 3B, Qwen 2.5 3B) that pass static safety audits but become vulnerable to latent attacks, measured by a Latent Vulnerability Score (LVS) 2.5 to 3.1 times higher than the bases. These attacks caused harmful compliance in 54 to 86% of prompts, compared to 3 to 48% for the original models, while random perturbations had minimal effect.

item.title: Researchers identify and manipulate a latent persona direction causing emergent misalignment in Qwen2.5 language models, with effects varying by fine-tuning method and model capacity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied emergent misalignment (EM) in Qwen2.5 language models, where fine-tuning on narrow harmful data induces broad misbehavior mediated by a latent persona direction in the model's weights. They demonstrated that transplanting this persona direction into related models induces misalignment, while ablating it reduces misalignment effects. The recruitment of this persona depends on the fine-tuning method and model capacity, with low-rank parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) more likely to recruit it than full supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The study found that steering training away from this persona direction can paradoxically increase misalignment, indicating that removing the direction is not a universal solution. The researchers also showed that recruitment of the persona can be screened for and selectively prevented, improving model behavior and code coherence. These findings highlight the complex, conditional role of latent directions in emergent misalignment and suggest methods to detect and mitigate such behaviors in large language models.

item.title: Researchers propose Truncated Jump Sampling to accelerate diffusion model generation by 20-70% without retraining or architecture changes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Truncated Jump Sampling (TJS), a method that leverages endpoint decodability to estimate clean samples early in diffusion and flow matching model sampling, reducing neural function evaluations by 20-70% across multiple benchmarks. TJS stops the ODE sampler at an early-exit time and decodes the sample without requiring retraining, distillation, or trajectory redesign. This approach maintains near-matched sample quality while providing inference acceleration without modifying existing model trajectories or architectures.

item.title: Researchers develop Fast Fourier Convolution ResNet for automated ECG interval measurement and wave delineation, evaluating accuracy on 10,646 clinical 12-lead ECGs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present an automated system using Fast Fourier Convolution ResNet (FFCResNet) to measure ECG intervals such as PR, QRS duration, and QT/QTc, addressing limitations of prior studies that focused on small curated datasets. The system was evaluated on a large cohort of 10,646 clinical 12-lead ECGs, providing comprehensive statistical analysis including bias, limits of agreement, and rhythm-stratified error metrics. The approach uses three per-wave models trained on six public databases with ECG-specific augmentation, achieving mean absolute errors of 17.5 ms for QT interval and 14.8 ms for QRS duration, with biases within or near inter-observer variability for sinus rhythms. Rhythm-stratified analysis showed higher errors in supraventricular tachycardias compared to sinus rhythms. Wave segmentation performance was high, with Dice scores above 95% internally and above 74% across databases, indicating robust delineation capabilities.

item.title: Researchers propose ACE-GraphRAG, an adaptive context policy layer for Hierarchical GraphRAG that refines multi-resolution knowledge retrieval to improve multi-hop QA and summarization tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce ACE-GraphRAG, an inference-time context policy layer designed to address the representation-inference gap in Hierarchical Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) by adapting context construction to better suit individual queries. The approach uses Parallel Differential Retrieval to gather supplementary evidence from factual and semantic branches, consolidating this with the initial context while preserving provenance and abstraction levels. Two variants, Full-ACE and Adaptive-ACE, apply these policies uniformly or selectively based on task and query topology. ACE-GraphRAG was evaluated on datasets including HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and UltraDomain subsets, showing improved performance over existing RAG and GraphRAG baselines in multi-hop question answering and query-focused summarization. Ablation studies support treating context construction as a dynamic, task-dependent inference policy rather than a fixed procedure.

item.title: Researchers propose SciStyleBench to diagnose and reduce stylistic bias in LLM-based scientific idea evaluation, showing improved substance recognition and ranking robustness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce SciStyleBench, a benchmark comprising three components-SciStyleStage, SciStyleMetrics, and SciStyleExtractor-to assess and mitigate the influence of writing style on large language models (LLMs) when evaluating scientific ideas. Their experiments reveal that direct LLM judges are sensitive to stylistic variations and struggle to accurately assess scientific substance, while the SciStyleExtractor module improves evaluation by separating style from content. SciStyleBench applies controlled stylistic changes to 600 scientific ideas across various contexts and measures effects using indices like Style Bias Index and Substance Recognition Rate. The study finds that incorporating style awareness reduces stylistic bias and enhances the robustness of idea evaluation, suggesting that effective scientific idea assessment by LLMs requires invariance to style without losing sensitivity to substantive content.

item.title: Researchers introduce LEAP, a scalable reinforcement learning framework with adaptive pruning for efficient GPU kernel code generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present LEAP (Lean Environment-Feedback via Adaptive Pruning), a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework designed to improve code generation for low-level GPU kernel programming. LEAP addresses challenges like sparse binary rewards and high compilation latency by dynamically pruning simple or catastrophic tasks, focusing computational resources on complex tasks to enhance learning efficiency. LEAP incorporates Difficulty-Conditioned Pruning and a Rank-Based Reward system that penalizes inefficiency on simple prompts while maximizing learning on difficult ones. Empirical results demonstrate that LEAP achieves faster convergence, better initial proficiency, and stronger multi-turn debugging resilience compared to unpruned baselines, offering a practical approach for reinforcement learning in low-level hardware accelerator code generation.

item.title: Researchers propose Meta-Persona Anchoring and Sequential Temperature Scaling to reduce response homogeneity in large language models, achieving diversity closer to human levels [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent study addresses the problem of homogeneity in large language models (LLMs), where models tend to produce highly similar responses even to open-ended questions, a phenomenon called the "Artificial Hivemind." Researchers propose a method combining Meta-Persona Anchoring, which prompts the model to adopt unique personas, with Filtered Temperature Scaling, a two-stage sampling process to increase response diversity. Evaluations on advanced open-weight models with around 20 billion parameters show a significant reduction in semantic convergence, lowering average response similarity from approximately 0.85 to 0.65. The approach uses a dual-stage generation process: first, the model selects an idiosyncratic persona to anchor its responses; second, it applies top-p filtering followed by extreme temperature scaling to explore a broader probability distribution. This method effectively reduces the gap between artificial mode collapse and human-level diversity in AI-generated text. The researchers have released their implementation as an open-source framework to encourage wider adoption and more diverse AI deployments.

item.title: Systematic review finds gaps in integrating Explainable AI with EU Right to Explanation under GDPR and AI Act, proposes framework and research agenda [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A systematic review of literature from 2024 onward examines how Explainable AI (XAI) aligns with the European Union's Right to Explanation, focusing on GDPR Article 15(1)(h) and Article 86 of the AI Act. The study identifies a significant gap between legal requirements and technical implementations, noting frequent misunderstandings of the legal basis and limited engagement with key court rulings. The authors introduce an Addressee/Purpose Framework to clarify explanation form and content and propose a four-phase blueprint for operationalizing the Right to Explanation. The review analyzed 57 relevant papers from an initial pool of 2,643, finding only 19 that substantively integrate legal and technical perspectives. It highlights three main issues: misidentification of GDPR provisions, lack of consideration of the Court of Justice of the European Union's Dun & Bradstreet judgment, and conflation of explanation form and content. The authors also outline six open research questions, warning that without interdisciplinary progress, the Right to Explanation risks remaining a formal obligation without practical technical solutions.

item.title: Study analyzes complexity collapse in atomic concept learning via hypercube and hyperplane geometry, revealing localized complexity patterns and equivalence class structures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This paper examines atomic concept learning by exploring the geometric structure of hypercubes and hyperplanes formed by ground instances. It finds that complexity is not uniform but organized along hyperplanes, with most collapsing into a finite number of equivalence classes except for the full diagonal, which shows unbounded complexity growth. This geometric pattern reflects the underlying logical and reduction-theoretic properties of the concepts. The study provides detailed analyses of binary and ternary cases, introduces a taxonomy of hyperplane behaviors in higher dimensions, and explains how complexity is concentrated rather than evenly distributed across the instance space. These insights offer a new perspective on constrained hypothesis spaces and structured classification in concept learning.

item.title: Researchers present an evidence-grounded multimodal pipeline to construct provenance-rich knowledge graphs from multi-lecture videos, integrating transcripts, OCR, and vision-language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed a multimodal pipeline that processes lecture videos by transcribing speech, extracting slide text and diagrams via OCR, and applying vision-language models to identify concepts and relationships supported by multiple evidence sources. The system validates and canonicalizes these mentions into a knowledge graph, demonstrated on three neural-network lectures with high coverage and retrieval accuracy. The contribution focuses on an auditable construction method rather than achieving state-of-the-art performance.

item.title: Researchers find surrogate substitution preserves PHI detectability across 11 detectors and 7 languages with minimal recall loss [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated structure-preserving de-identification methods that replace protected health information (PHI) with realistic surrogates to maintain clinical text fluency and tool functionality. They tested whether downstream PHI detectors could still identify surrogates on masked spans using a multi-detector equivalence protocol across 11 detectors, 7 benchmarks, and 7 languages, analyzing 1,750 documents. The study found recall on masked spans decreased slightly from 76.1% to 74.9%, a change statistically equivalent to zero within a ±2-point margin, with detector rankings preserved. Residual recall loss was attributed to malformed or out-of-distribution surrogates rather than detector performance degradation. The researchers released evaluation subsets, scoring code, and an interactive dashboard to support auditing of structure-preserving transformations.

item.title: Researchers find that LLM benchmark gains reflect both new and previously reachable answers, with realization and reachability not always increasing together across models from 0.5B to 31B parameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A new study distinguishes between realized and reachable answers in large language model (LLM) benchmarks, showing that performance gains can come from producing answers already within reach rather than new capabilities. The researchers audited 43 model-task settings under fixed conditions and found that inference-time layer routing can expand reachability, but answer-blind methods do not retain these gains. Silencing specific MLP blocks repaired many failures where reachable answers failed to appear. The study also tested whether training expands reachability and found that in most cases, deployed performance improved while the reachable ceiling remained flat or declined, indicating that realized performance and reachability do not always change together. The authors suggest that claims of LLM capability expansion should report both realized performance and reachability under matched evaluation conditions. The code for their analysis is publicly available.

item.title: Researchers test context-length effects in long-context LLM benchmarks using distractor-aware truncation to separate signal loss from context window size [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated the impact of context length on language model performance by comparing naive truncation, which removes content from the middle of prompts, with a distractor-aware protocol that preserves task-relevant information. They tested multiple models including three Claude variants and GPT-5.5 across several benchmarks, finding that naive truncation caused performance to collapse due to loss of answer-bearing content, while distractor-aware truncation preserved or improved performance by maintaining relevant signals. The study showed that naive truncation results do not measure true context-window effects but rather reflect how often the answer is removed. This finding was consistent across different models and benchmarks, indicating that future research on context length must carefully distinguish between signal and distractor content to avoid ambiguous conclusions about the effects of context size on model performance.

item.title: AI World Cup 2026 benchmark evaluates 10 large language models on full FIFA World Cup tournament prediction using uniform data and scoring [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The AI World Cup benchmark tested ten large language models (LLMs) on a single pre-tournament forecast of the entire 2026 FIFA World Cup, using the same data snapshot, prompt, JSON schema, and scoring method. GPT-5.5 Thinking ranked first with 744 points, correctly predicting Spain as champion, followed by GPT-5.5, Gemini, and Qwen 3.7. The final rankings correlated strongly with knockout stage performance but not with group-stage accuracy or self-reported confidence. The benchmark covered predictions of group-stage scores, rankings, knockout brackets, final placements, confidence levels, and explanations. While Claude Sonnet 4.6 had the highest group-stage match accuracy, it placed sixth overall, highlighting differences between forecasting entire tournaments and individual matches. The study released all benchmark materials, raw responses, and scoring code to support replication and future research.

item.title: ChartAnno benchmark evaluates 10 multimodal large language models on chart annotation generation using 1,200 real-world charts with code and instructions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce ChartAnno, a benchmark designed to assess multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on the task of generating annotations for existing charts, a complex task involving semantic interpretation and message inference. The benchmark includes 1,200 real-world charts paired with code and annotation instructions at varying levels of specificity. Ten representative MLLMs were evaluated under different input conditions: chart code alone, chart code with chart image, and chart image only. Results indicate that proprietary models generally outperform open-source ones, though the gap is narrowing. More detailed instructions lead to better annotation quality, while current models struggle most with inferring abstract intent. Including chart images provides limited overall improvement, mainly enhancing design-related aspects. The study highlights chart annotation generation as a challenging task requiring both semantic understanding and effective design, with code and data planned for future release.

item.title: Researchers introduce Cue-GRPO to redistribute credit in reinforcement learning by accounting for solution rarity, improving performance on Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The paper presents Cue-GRPO, a method that addresses credit concentration in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by redistributing positive advantages based on the rarity of solution clusters. This approach counters the bias where frequently sampled correct solutions accumulate disproportionate credit, while rare solutions receive less. Cue-GRPO uses deterministic Strategy Cues to partition verified-correct traces without auxiliary model inference, enhancing performance on competition mathematics tasks such as AIME with minimal training overhead compared to GRPO. Experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct demonstrate that Cue-GRPO yields the largest gains at high sampling budgets. Additional tests with Credit Redistribution under Judge Partitions suggest the mechanism can also work with judge-derived partitions. The authors provide code for their method, supporting structure-level credit redistribution as a practical design axis for RLVR in mathematical problem-solving contexts.

item.title: Researchers introduce hybrid LLM-augmented reinforcement learning agents combining LLM-driven planning with RL action optimization for complex sequential decision tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a hybrid agent architecture that integrates large language models (LLMs) for high-level planning and reinforcement learning (RL) for low-level action optimization to address challenges in long-horizon sequential decision tasks. The LLM generates subgoals and structured plans, while the RL component refines actions through environment interaction. Experiments demonstrate that this approach improves sample efficiency, success rates, and action coherence compared to using LLMs or RL alone, suggesting a promising direction for more capable autonomous systems.

item.title: Researchers propose CASE framework to enhance tabular learners with context-aware semantic embeddings using a Gemma 3-based Tabular Language Model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce CASE (Context-Aware Semantic Embeddings), a framework that integrates semantic understanding from Large Language Models with tabular learners by pre-filling the KV cache of a custom Gemma 3-based Tabular Language Model using representative dataset samples. This approach dynamically contextualizes row embeddings to resolve semantic ambiguities and anchor representations in domain-specific contexts. Experiments on benchmarks including CARTE, TextTab, and TabArena show that CASE significantly improves tabular learner performance on semantically rich datasets, especially in low-data scenarios.

item.title: Researchers benchmark AI scientist capabilities using fast-moving real-world domains Formula 1 car design and Magic: The Gathering deck building [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose using complex, adversarial, fast-moving real-world domains to benchmark AI scientists' abilities in reasoning, novelty, and hypothesis formulation. They test this approach in Formula 1 car design for the 2026 season and Magic: The Gathering deck building, comparing AI-generated ideas to expert innovations and tournament decks. Models produced plausible outputs but matched only a fraction of real-world expert solutions, with GPT-5.2 identifying 10 of 40 F1 innovations and Gemini 3 Flash recovering 5 of 7 new-set cards in MTG. The study suggests AI scientists face challenges not in generating ideas but in filtering, prioritizing, and producing coherent novelty.

item.title: FOUND-AF benchmarks nine ECG foundation models for atrial fibrillation detection across four datasets, finding ECGFounder offers best accuracy and efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: FOUND-AF introduces a unified benchmarking framework to evaluate pretrained ECG foundation models for atrial fibrillation (AF) detection under consistent conditions. The study assessed nine models from five families using four heterogeneous ECG datasets with standardized preprocessing and a fixed classifier to ensure fair comparison. ECGFounder consistently delivered the strongest overall performance, balancing accuracy, model size, inference time, and memory usage. This framework aids in selecting robust and computationally efficient ECG models for AF detection across diverse clinical settings.

item.title: Researchers train offline decision agents to plan oncology clinical trial portfolios using a dataset of 31.7k records across 45 historical programs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers framed oncology clinical development as an offline decision-making problem where an agent predicts six-month trial portfolios based on available data. They constructed a temporal dataset combining 31,700 heterogeneous public records into 881 offline decision episodes covering 45 historical drug programs. Four offline training objectives were compared against four large language model agents using date-gated retrieval across various data splits. Models trained offline outperformed non-fine-tuned baselines, with reward-weighted behavioral cloning achieving the highest indication and strict F1 scores. These findings suggest structured offline learning can effectively teach agents to plan clinical experiments.

item.title: Researchers derive a closed-form Jacobian bound for attention sub-blocks and test cross-layer interaction under weight-space ablation on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This paper extends prior work on activation patching and weight-space ablation by analyzing cross-layer interactions in transformers beyond single residual blocks. The authors derive an exact decomposition of interactions from ablating carriers across multiple layers, isolate a cross-layer remainder term, and provide a closed-form Jacobian bound for the attention sub-block, which they verify against real pretrained weights from Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. They also identify an emergent circuit for indirect object identification in the model using activation patching, finding mixed results on collapse, dissociation, and interaction across layers.

item.title: Researchers present competition-aware request dispatch framework for real-time ad exchanges that reduces DSP request volume by 34.2% and increases net revenue by 4.6% in production experiments [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers developed a competition-aware request dispatch system for real-time bidding ad exchanges that uses bid prediction and probabilistic forwarding to selectively send requests to demand-side platforms (DSPs). This approach addresses over-distribution issues where DSPs throttle participation due to compute and budget constraints, weakening auction outcomes. The system adapts per-DSP thresholds through lightweight policy optimization to handle changing market conditions. Tested on a production platform processing over 20 billion daily requests, the multi-DSP deployment cut DSP request volume by 34.2% while boosting net revenue by 4.6% over a 14-day period after initial adaptation. Further analysis revealed significant variation across traffic segments and DSPs, indicating that the policy improves monetized outcomes by leveraging comparative advantages without increasing overall request volume.

item.title: Researchers propose a black-box diagnostic to measure if increased output diversity in LLM collectives corresponds to genuine epistemic revision [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This study introduces a method to assess whether interventions that increase the diversity of outputs in large language model (LLM) collectives lead to actual changes in their epistemic stance rather than mere reformulations of the same premise. The diagnostic operates solely on generated text, measuring output dispersion with a Coherence Index and epistemic revision through per-turn stance annotations. Evaluations on two five-agent LLM configurations, gpt-4o-mini and gemini-2.5-flash, reveal that conditional dissent improves false-premise recovery in gpt-4o-mini but not in gemini-2.5-flash, where dissent often preserves false premises through reformulation rather than concession. The authors recommend reporting stance shifts and premise-preservation rates alongside accuracy in future studies.

item.title: Researchers identify and address the faithfulness-safety tension in large reasoning models using a new dataset and targeted reasoning replacement technique [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have identified a tension in large reasoning models (LRMs) between faithfulness-where model outputs strictly follow their reasoning traces-and safety, which requires rejecting unsafe reasoning. They introduced HazMart, a human-written dataset simulating an autonomous AI shopkeeper, and developed Targeted Reasoning Replacement (TRR), a novel method that intervenes in reasoning chains to substitute unsafe or illogical thoughts. Experiments showed that DeepSeek-R1-Llama-70B has high faithfulness but lower safety, while QwQ-32B is safer but less faithful. Mechanistic analysis revealed anti-correlated internal representations linked to these properties, and representation steering was demonstrated to improve safety without compromising capabilities.

item.title: Researchers develop scalable method to compute Halpern-Pearl actual causes for neural network predictions using Boolean Structural Causal Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers address the challenge of explaining neural network predictions by formalizing explanations as Halpern-Pearl actual causes and modeling input dependencies with Boolean Structural Causal Models (SCMs). They apply bound propagation and branch-and-bound techniques to compute these causes, providing formal guarantees of completeness and minimality while outperforming brute-force and ILP baselines in scalability. Their method handles search spaces with up to 2.3×10^{13} candidate cause-contingency pairs on SCMs with up to 28 nodes within a 180-second per-instance budget. A case study demonstrates that ignoring input dependencies inflates the number of reported causes, with 14.9% identified as spurious under their SCM framework.

item.title: Researchers propose socially grounded agentic AI design using social theory to coordinate multiple perspectives beyond unified value alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers argue that AI alignment must move beyond optimizing a single set of values to recognize and coordinate multiple legitimate perspectives in diverse social contexts. They propose using social theory to understand perspectives as structured by roles and power dynamics, informing AI system design with role-based representations and context-sensitive evaluation. The paper outlines a design framework for agentic AI systems that align not only outputs but also the internal processes like role activations and feedback loops that produce those outputs. This approach reframes pluralistic alignment as a problem of socially grounded coordination rather than mere output diversification, with directions for future empirical evaluation in real-world settings.

item.title: KernelBrain: Coarse-to-Fine, Budget-Aware Search for Agentic GPU Kernel Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02611v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automating GPU kernel optimization remains difficult in practice: generated variants can violate correctness constraints, runtime measurements are noisy, and search often stalls early. We present a practical optimization agent that combines LLM-guided mutation, adaptive resource allocation, policy-gated evaluation, and profiler-informed diagnosis. The system screens many candidates with low-cost evaluation and allocates higher-fidelity budget only to promising survivors to optimize and evolve GPU kernels. On important Triton kernel generation tasks, this design improves both kernel quality and search efficiency, reaching 0.88x-6.72x speedup over PyTorch and up to 1.4x speedup over the state-of-the-art kernel agent, with up to 48% lower optimization time.

item.title: OncoTriad-QA: A Patient-Level Radiology-Pathology-Genomics Benchmark for Pan-Cancer Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cancer diagnosis and characterization require integrating complementary evidence from radiology, pathology, genomics, and clinical metadata. However, most medical large language model (LLM) and vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks focus on isolated modalities or narrow image-text tasks, leaving patient-level oncology assessment across multiple evidence streams largely untested. We introduce OncoTriad-QA, a patient-level radiology-pathology-genomics benchmark for pan-cancer question answering. OncoTriad-QA contains 86.1k semantic questions across 9,281 TCGA patient cases from 32 cancer cohorts, aligning CT/MRI radiology, whole-slide histopathology, somatic mutations, copy-number alterations, DNA methylation, bulk RNA-seq, and clinical metadata. Case-specific annotations are constructed through a source-grounded LLM-assisted pipeline using curated labels, diagnostic reports, molecular profiles, and modality-derived evidence as primary sources of truth, with automated consistency checks and clinician review. We also introduce OncoVLM, a reference multimodal model that maps modality-native radiology, pathology, DNA methylation, and RNA-seq evidence into an LLM interface through learned projectors. Experiments show that existing general-purpose and medical LLMs remain limited on comprehensive pan-cancer QA, especially when questions require integrating imaging findings, tumor morphology, and molecular evidence. After fine-tuning on OncoTriad-QA, OncoVLM exceeds MedGemma-4B by an average of 10.7 points when using MCQ accuracy and BERTScore-F1, with consistent gains across multiple-choice and open-ended questions under radiology-only, pathology-only, and all-available settings. These results demonstrate the benchmark's value for training and evaluating models for integrated cancer question answering.

item.title: Evaluating OpenAI's Privacy Filter: Cross-Lingual, Cross-Domain PII Detection Across 42 Benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the first independent, systematic evaluation of OpenAI's Privacy Filter (OPF), a 1.5B-parameter bidirectional PII detector, across 42 synthetic benchmarks spanning 22 languages and 5 domains. Zero-shot, OPF achieves F1=0.855 on AI4Privacy and 0.464 on SPY medical, outperforming Presidio (0.431, 0.273) and XLM-RoBERTa (0.269, 0.111) on PII-annotated benchmarks; on multilingual NER, XLM-RoBERTa leads OPF on all 13 Indic and non-Latin languages. GPT-4o leads on medical, legal, and financial PII (SPY: 0.643 avg, Gretel: 0.527), while OPF leads on structured synthetic PII (0.71 avg) and customer support (0.60). OPF degrades sharply when PII is embedded in narrative prose: F1=0.04--0.57 on NER benchmarks and collapse for non-Latin scripts (Arabic: 0.04, Cyrillic: 0.03). Error analysis shows OPF is strongest on structurally regular PII types (email: 0.78, phone: 0.76) and weakest on culturally variable ones (person: 0.40, address: 0.49), and is recall-biased on customer-support and medical/legal PII (P=0.31--0.54, R=0.70--0.85); global precision spans 0.31--0.86 across all domains.

item.title: Knowing the Form, Not the Function: Automatically Auditing Answer--Authority Decoupling in Legal Benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Legal benchmarks typically score final answers even when models also state legal authority. We test whether answer correctness can serve as a proxy for authority grounding. Under ordinary reasoning prompts that did not request statutory citations, four LLMs spontaneously produced authority markers across 238 Taiwan bar-examination items. Because each item has a verified governing provision, we automatically audit answer correctness and authority grounding jointly. The two dimensions dissociate in both directions. In criminal law, 24.0--42.4\% of valid responses were answer-correct but missed the gold authority, while 15.2--21.7\% were answer-incorrect but cited it. A separate statutory-retrieval probe and a permissive citation-abstention intervention further show that answer and citation behavior can move separately at the output level. Because this mismatch arises without adversarial or inconsistency-inducing prompting, answer-only scoring treats naturally occurring gold-authority misses as complete benchmark successes. Because statutory authority is structurally extractable and externally verifiable, the failure can be measured automatically. A preliminary PRC civil-law extension also observes citation-unrequested authority marking, motivating a full cross-jurisdictional joint audit. We therefore propose joint answer--authority evaluation for statute-grounded legal benchmarks.

item.title: Speculative Correction: Draft-then-Refine Decoding for Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can revise tokens bidirectionally, but standard decoding procedures often adapt them to left-to-right generation by producing text block by block. We study a simple plug-and-play inference pattern: first generate a complete draft, then refine the full response using bidirectional diffusion. Using LLaDA2.1-Flash and LLaDA2.1-Mini, we evaluate two configurations. In Flash-Flash, the same Flash model serves as both drafter and refiner, testing whether an existing model can improve its own block-autoregressive output through global refinement. In Mini-Flash, inspired by speculative decoding, we introduce speculative correction: Mini drafts a full response, and Flash revises it as an editable initialization. Flash-Flash improves GSM8K-384 accuracy from 0.848 to 0.899 while running 1.20 times faster than the selected Flash block-autoregressive baseline, and improves MBPP-384 from 0.545 to 0.693. Latency-window-matched Flash-only controls indicate that these gains persist after targeted tuning of block-autoregressive decoding. Causal ablations indicate that completed drafts provide useful initializations: refinement from a fully masked span performs poorly, full global refinement provides a clear additional gain on GSM8K, and local refinement captures much of the gain on MBPP and MATH. Mini-Flash provides useful quality-latency trade-offs, including MATH-384 performance of 0.294 versus 0.300 for Flash while running 2.17 times faster. These results support a Pareto-frontier interpretation rather than the claim that the heterogeneous cascade uniformly matches Flash quality. Overall, same-model draft-and-refine provides evidence that bidirectional refinement is a useful decoding primitive for DLMs, while speculative correction demonstrates a training-free route to fast DLM generation.

item.title: Deep Divide-and-Reduce in Symbolic Regression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02628v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) is the task of discovering underlying patterns from data and representing them using mathematical expressions. Current machine learning approaches to SR often lack a profound understanding of the intrinsic mathematical and physical principles governing these expressions. While the pioneering AI Feynman method leverages the mathematical properties underlying the data, its expression simplification mechanism suffers from a narrow scope of applicability and is prone to failure on complex equations. Furthermore, its underlying mechanisms rely heavily on brute-force searches for sub-expressions, severely limiting its practical utility. Through rigorous mathematical deduction and proofs, we propose our method, Deep Divide and Reduce in Symbolic Regression (DDRSR). DDRSR fundamentally broadens the applicability of expression decomposition and reduction, circumvents the need for brute-force sub-structure searches, and ensures both wider versatility and strict theoretical correctness. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that these theoretical principles yield significant advantages in both expression decomposition and numerical regression tasks. Finally, we discuss the applicable scenarios and inherent limitations of this paradigm, alongside promising directions for future research.

item.title: Multimodal Auto-regressive Transformer Surrogate for Modeling Variable Operations and Quantifying Uncertainty in Geological Carbon Storage [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The use of variable well perforation and injection strategies can improve the efficiency of geological carbon storage operations. We develop a new multimodal auto-regressive transformer surrogate to model these operations under geological uncertainty. A modified SEAM CO2 geomodel, which involves a faulted system with three stacked aquifers, is considered. The two injection wells are perforated in stages, from bottom to top, with the stage durations and individual well injection rates treated as control variables. The surrogate model processes three input modalities - the 3D geomodel, scalar parameters characterizing relative permeability functions, and control variables - through separate encoders. These are fused via self-attention in a transformer encoder, and a temporal decoder generates predictions auto-regressively through encoder-decoder cross-attention. The surrogate is trained, using 4000 GEOS flow simulations, to predict saturation and pressure at monitoring locations, total injected and mobile CO2 mass, and saturation footprints. For a new test set, involving randomly sampled geomodels and control variables, the surrogate achieves a median saturation MAE of 0.028 and median relative errors of 0.2-5% for the other quantities of interest. Importantly, it captures the switch from rate to bottom-hole-pressure control. The surrogate model is used within a hierarchical Markov chain Monte Carlo data assimilation procedure for a synthetic true model under three operational strategies. Substantial uncertainty reduction is achieved for key metaparameters, particularly the fault permeabilities. Posterior predictions for saturation footprints and total injected and mobile CO2 mass are also shown to be generally consistent with true model results.

item.title: Verifier-Guided Model Discovery for Physical Dynamical Systems with Pretrained Symbolic Transformers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable forecasting of nonlinear physical systems underpins scientific discovery and engineering decision-making. Yet high-fidelity simulations are prohibitively costly, and machine-learning surrogates can be opaque and encode assumptions about system dynamics, limiting generalizability. Pretrained transformers mapping synthetic ODE trajectories to equations offer interpretable alternatives, promising transfer without system-specific equation knowledge. Transferring them reliably to high-dimensional physical data, however, remains an open challenge. We develop a verifier-guided (VG) workflow around ODEFormer as a symbolic backbone, using dynamical and physical-admissibility criteria to select from a multi-trajectory candidate equation pool, enabling transfer. On canonical Van der Pol oscillators, VG outperforms the original ODEFormer workflow across held-out initial conditions. We then address vortex shedding, a phenomenon occurring in atmospheric and plasma systems of societal relevance, through coordinate reduction and symbolic discovery at fixed and varying Reynolds numbers. VG discovers fixed-parameter reduced-order equations that recover the fundamental shedding oscillator and higher harmonics without a wake-specific candidate library or prescribed Navier-Stokes structure, while the cross-parameter model generalizes to withheld regimes. Reconstruction fidelity alone did not determine symbolic discoverability, highlighting the importance of compatibility between latent dynamics and the backbone's pretraining distribution. This work establishes a verifier-guided neural-to-symbolic methodology for interpretable and physically auditable forecasting in the natural sciences.

item.title: CT-HEG: A Bidirectional, Timestamp-Attributed Event Graph for ICU In-Hospital Mortality Prediction - An Architectural Ablation Study [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate ICU mortality prediction requires modeling irregular clinical observations across heterogeneous entity types. Existing sequence models handle irregular sampling but ignore typed relational structure; existing graph models assume fixed-interval inputs. We introduce the Continuous-Time Heterogeneous EHR Graph (CT-HEG) schema and evaluate which architectural choices drive predictive performance. CT-HEG encodes each ICU stay as a typed, timestamped graph with three node types (visit, vital, lab_event) and 2D edge attributes (t_hours/48, value_norm) encoding timing and value without imputation. We instantiate CT-HEG as CHIRP-Net, a four-layer heterogeneous GATv2Conv network, evaluated on MIMIC-IV v3.1 (31,142 ICU stays, LOS>=48h, 13.4% mortality) with five seeds and bootstrapped confidence intervals, against logistic regression, mTAND, a Transformer, and GRU-D, plus an ablation study. CHIRP-Net achieved 5-seed mean AUROC 0.8449+/-0.0071 (AUPRC 0.4958+/-0.0209); the ensemble achieved AUROC 0.8618 (95% CI: 0.8485-0.8745). Removing reverse edges disconnected observation nodes from the visit readout, cutting AUROC by 0.1968+/-0.0073. Time-attentive edge features contributed 0.0247+/-0.0093 AUROC. Collapsing heterogeneous edge types into one relation (7x fewer parameters) outperformed the full model on all seeds. Post-calibration ECE was 0.0307. Temporal and demographic subgroup analyses were explored but not reported here, pending follow-up work. Bidirectional connectivity was necessary for the model to use its inputs at all, and CT-HEG was reasonably well calibrated after validation-fitted temperature scaling. These results support CT-HEG for irregular EHR data, while external validation, a pre-specified temporal evaluation, and a demographic fairness audit remain necessary before any claim of robustness. Code: https://github.com/nasiruddinstudents-ctrl/chirp-net-mimic-iv.

item.title: Single Canonical Prompts Underestimate LLM Safety's Surface-Form Sensitivity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02665v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A benchmark score is a measurement instrument, yet most benchmarks read each item at a single canonical surface form. We ask whether that reading is faithful: when an item's intent is held fixed and only its meaning-preserving surface form varies, does the canonical-form score estimate model behavior well, and how much of any variation is decoding/judge noise rather than signal? We instantiate this in safety, a high-stakes setting with no gold label to average toward. To avoid prior confounds, we pre-author the reformulations (refusal-free, mostly non-LLM: machine back-translation and a Matrix-Language-Frame code-switch generator) so an identical surface form reaches every model, score all responses with one human-anchored, vendor-neutral judge (Claude, kappa = 0.86 vs. human on unsafe compliance, stable across languages, cross-checked by GPT-4o), and verify intent preservation. On 370 seeds x 5 surface forms x 5 models, no single transformation is uniformly most dangerous (6 of 20 per-transformation McNemar tests survive correction, most protective). Yet evaluating only the canonical prompt underestimates unsafe compliance: the union of unsafe outcomes across forms exceeds even the worst single form by 3.3-12.9 pp, with bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero for all five models, and 5-13% of seeds safe on canonical are unsafe under some reformulation -- above a zero stochasticity floor (canonical resampled five times at temperature 0 gives 0/370 new exposures). The size of this gap is model-dependent (largest on Gemini 2.5 Pro). One form recovers only ~53% of a model's observed unsafe surface and about three reach 85% -- a redundancy characterization of this form set, not of a defined population. A benign control (XSTest) suggests the instability is bidirectional, though the benign and harmful pools are not item-matched. We release the dataset, code, and per-response labels.

item.title: dots.tts.edit: Precisely Controlled Speech Editing with a Continuous Autoregressive Model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02673v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech editing for content creation requires precise control over both what an edit should do and where it should apply. Free-form natural language provides a flexible interface for expressing edit requests, but its ambiguity may leave the intended operation, parameters, or target region underspecified. We study a precise and explicit interface for speech editing: a transcript-grounded structural edit instruction with XML-style tags explicitly specifies typed operations and localizes them to transcript spans or boundaries. This semantic timeline avoids explicit timestamp alignment and provides an externally inspectable contract for compositional edits. We instantiate the interface in dots.tts.edit, an editor adapted from the continuous autoregressive dots.tts foundation model. Four representative speech-creation controls cover lexical content, affective expression, pitch and speaking-rate delivery, and temporal phrasing through text, emotion, prosody, and pause editing. Task-specific data pipelines construct operation- and scope-controlled pairs while retaining source-derived context outside each target region. We further introduce doteBench, a bilingual evaluation suite that measures precise instruction following, local preservation, and audio quality across the four controls and their composition. Experiments show leading overall instruction following and local preservation across its five editing categories, while audio quality remains comparable to existing open-source systems. Across three Seed-TTS-Eval shards, the model shows negligible differences from the base model in zero-shot TTS recognition error rate and speaker similarity. The code and model will be released soon.

item.title: DenialRAG: Single-Document RAG Poisoning via Embedded Parametric Denial [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02678v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to corpus poisoning: an attacker who inserts a crafted document into the retrieval corpus can steer the underlying large language model (LLM) toward an attacker-chosen wrong answer. Prior single-document attacks typically avoid explicitly naming and refuting the correct answer inside the poisoned passage. In this paper, we examine a complementary design and propose \emph{DenialRAG}, a single-document poisoning attack that explicitly names the correct answer, denies it, and presents an attacker-controlled explanation for favoring the wrong answer. By placing both the correct answer and the corresponding poisoned answer inside the same retrieved passage, DenialRAG embeds the conflict directly into the context seen by the generator. We evaluate DenialRAG against four published single-document poisoning attacks across three open-domain question-answering datasets, eight target LLMs from four vendors, and five inference-time defenses. The results show that attack effectiveness is strongly model-dependent: DenialRAG achieves the highest attack success rate (ASR) on all three Mistral-7B datasets and remains effective on several other target LLMs, while other attacks dominate in some model regimes. Defense results show meaningful ASR reductions but non-uniform protection, with each defense leaving residual ASR in some settings. Component-level and cross-model analyses further identify the embedded denial as the most influential tested component and show that different poisoning mechanisms lose effectiveness at different rates across model groups. Together, these results show that RAG poisoning risk cannot be fully characterized by a single attack family or a single target model.

item.title: TraceCompiler: Skill-Guided Mining and Compilation of LLM Agent Traces into Mostly Deterministic Workflows [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02680v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tool-using language-model agents repeatedly rediscover procedures they have already executed, producing traces that mix reusable structure with retries, exploration, accidental ordering, and repeated lookups. We present TraceCompiler, a skill-guided system that mines clusters of noisy agent traces and compiles them into executable, mostly deterministic workflows. It admits an inter-tool dependency only when a consumer argument contains a value attributable uniquely to an earlier producer; every hard edge carries an auditable evidence tuple, and ambiguous relations are marked suspected and impose no ordering constraint. Bindings are classified as constants, user inputs, copied outputs, transforms, or residual LLM decisions. On T1, a mechanized form of the rule recovers producer-consumer dependencies at 0.928 precision and 0.943 recall over 15,775 def-use edges of its training split, against 0.711 F1 for adjacency and 0.712 for a frequency-thresholded directly-follows measure on identical data; the compiler skill run blind reaches 0.992 on 250 of those edges. On AppWorld we replay released trajectories in the deterministic simulator to recover masked return values and measure the rule against 563 token edges at 0.993 precision - a self-consistency check, since replay injects tokens by a related heuristic. We compile two recurring intents: a Venmo money-request intent reduces 34 observed API calls to 11 runtime calls and, under leave-one-out execution against the benchmark's own state tests, passes 15 of 21, the failing fold escalating rather than acting because its required branch was never observed; and a Spotify/Todoist intent the compiler correctly refuses to compile, because an irreversible side effect is under-determined. We measure call reduction but not offline compilation cost, so we claim no net efficiency result.

item.title: Learning Molecular Representations from Cellular Phenotypes with Structure Preservation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phenotypic drug discovery enables the discovery of functional relationships between molecular structures and cellular responses. However, existing multimodal representation learning methods often optimize cross-modal alignment without considering the intrinsic organization of chemical space, resulting in distorted molecular representations and loss of structural information. We propose \textbf{PhenMol}, a structure-preserving framework for phenotype-aware molecular representation learning. PhenMol disentangles molecular and cellular representations into shared and private components, enabling phenotype-guided alignment while preserving chemical structures through a dedicated molecular branch. This design integrates cellular phenotype information without disrupting molecular neighborhood organization. Experiments on approximately $3.04 \times 10^{4}$ molecule--cell morphology pairs demonstrate that PhenMol improves molecular property prediction across 270 bioactivity tasks, molecule--phenotype retrieval, and clinical trial outcome prediction. Moreover, ECFP4-based structural analysis shows that PhenMol better preserves molecular neighborhoods and reduces embedding distortion compared with existing multimodal alignment methods. These results highlight the importance of structure-aware constraints in multimodal molecular representation learning and provide an effective approach for integrating cellular phenotypes with chemical knowledge for drug discovery.

item.title: Output-Aware Rotation for INT2 KV-Cache Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The key-value (KV) cache has become a major memory and bandwidth bottleneck in long-context large language model inference, making ultra-low-bit quantization increasingly important. However, existing rotation-based INT2 methods optimize cache statistics or proxy errors before the complete attention readout, even though the model is ultimately affected by the error propagated through attention and the output projection $W_O$. To address this mismatch, we propose \textit{OptR}, an output-aware rotation method that minimizes post-$W_O$ attention-output error. OptR decomposes the post-$W_O$ attention-output error into key- and value-induced terms and learns per-head orthogonal corrections through the full INT2 quantization and attention path. OptR further applies an attention-equivalent key reparameterization to reduce large channel-wise offsets without changing the softmax distribution. Across three models and five reasoning and coding benchmarks, OptR consistently improves both QuaRot and OSCAR and strengthens long-context retrieval, while preserving the paged KV-cache format with negligible inference overhead.

item.title: Measuring Explainer Stability via Attribution Separability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attribution methods (AMs) assign an importance score to each feature and are widely adopted to explain black-box models. However, most methods can produce variable attribution scores due to stochastic components in their definition. In this paper, we propose a distribution-based framework to capture the stability of attribution scores. In particular, our approach allows to understand the degree of separability in the ranked attribution vector and obtain the largest index for which a feature ranking remains reliable. We further extend this framework to compare AMs based on the robustness of their rankings across a dataset. Through experiments, we demonstrate how to apply our method to evaluate explainer stability. Overall, our approach provides a complementary criterion for evaluating the stability of AMs.

item.title: NANQ: Noise-Floor-Aware Mixed-Precision Non-Uniform Quantization for Analog Compute-in-Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) enables energy-efficient neural network inference, but device variation and read noise can severely degrade low-bit quantized models. Existing CIM-oriented quantization methods mainly minimize ideal quantization error, ignoring the hardware noise floor and thus causing inefficient precision allocation. We propose NANQ, a noise-aware mixed-precision non-uniform quantization framework for analog CIM. NANQ models magnitude-dependent weight noise from measured responses of an eFlash CIM array and converts the noise profile into an adaptive quantization density, assigning finer resolution to low-noise regions while avoiding ineffective precision in noise-dominated regions. It further assigns layer-wise bit-widths by identifying each layer's precision saturation point under hardware noise using a unified threshold. On-chip experiments on an eFlash CIM SoC show that, under 2-bit weight-magnitude quantization, NANQ improves vision-model accuracy by 8.05 percentage points and reduces language-model PPL by 54.7% on average over PowerQuant. Mixed-precision NANQ captures most of the gains obtainable from additional quantization resources with only 3.2-3.8 equivalent bits.

item.title: Can Training Logs Make Model Comparisons More Precise? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Comparing stochastically trained models requires estimating both a performance difference and its uncertainty from repeated runs. We study whether training logs from those same runs can make such comparisons more precise. Because training-log covariates are produced during training rather than measured before it, we use arm-specific covariate adjustment: each model is adjusted only with statistics from its own runs, and the raw mean difference remains the reported effect. In a vision study spanning three architectures and three datasets, simple adjustments based on early training logs often reduce uncertainty in model comparisons. The main limitation is covariate selection. Broadly searching the log pool for the most correlated statistic often adds more noise than it removes, even when useful statistics exist in hindsight. Training logs therefore appear useful for more precise model comparisons, but only when the adjustment avoids large selection noise.

item.title: Designing a Good Virtual Node: Addressable and Cardinality-Preserving Global Memory for Message Passing Architectures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Virtual nodes give message-passing neural networks a simple global communication route, but the standard node--VN--node pipeline compresses the graph into one homogeneous state and broadcasts it identically to every node. Building on the Two-Radius analysis of Mishayev et al., we ask how auxiliary virtual memory can relieve this finite-capacity bottleneck without self-attention. We identify two requirements. First, the global memory should be factorized into independently writable and readable states: this can be achieved using addressable cross-attention slots. Second, addressability alone does not preserve multiplicity, because softmax attention is invariant to uniform replication.
